doc.title: Hentoff Nat — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Charles Edward Smith, Jazzmen and Roger Pryor Dodge
summary: Smith and Jazzmen inspired him to write; they discuss whether anyone made a living writing on jazz, and Dodge, whom he never met.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Critics, polls and the jazz press

blocks.x: Let’s start to talk about these writers and people whose footsteps you followed in. You mentioned Charles Edward Smith. I’d like to talk about George Frazier and Roger Pryor Dodge and people like that. Let’s start with Smith. What’s his place from two perspectives: (a) you, the young 20-year-old, in 1945?; and (b) from our perspective today? Where do you see Charles Edward Smith?

I wish people read him now. I don’t think it’s a name that would mean much, even to some of the people – younger people who write about the music. He and Fred Ramsey, who was also a very good writer and researcher and traveler, they wrote a book called Jazzmen, I think. I read that pretty much as it came out. That was like reading a romance. They made not only the musicians come alive – obviously they talked to various – a lot of people – but you got the whole ambience, the sense of what New Orleans was like and then Chicago and all that. For example, he once wrote about Pee Wee Russell, whom I later got to know very well – Pee Wee was not the easiest guy to get to talk, but you learned the full-blown Pee Wee Russell from reading Charles Edward Smith. That influenced me in the sense that I wanted to be that kind of writer. I don’t think I ever got as fluid as he was. He was a very important figure.
We talked on the phone several times. I think I met him once. Yeah, as a matter of fact, I did meet him down here in the Village.
Did he live in New York? He didn’t live in Boston?
I don’t know. I think he lived in New York.
He was a writer by trade. He made a living writing.

I assume he did. He was involved in a number of books. He did liner notes and the like. You see, in those days, though, I don’t know that anybody made a full-time living out of writing about jazz. Ralph Gleason in San Francisco did to a certain extent, but he wrote about the whole cultural music scene, etc. Leonard Feather probably came closest to a writer who made a living out of writing about jazz.
Were you aware of Roger Pryor Dodge at that time? Or was that someone . . .?
Roger Pryor Dodge. Was that someone at that time that you knew about, or was it later?
He lived where I lived for a while, at 25 Fifth Avenue, but we never met.
When you go back and read his early writings, it’s remarkably prescient, from the ’20s.
I ought to, but he’s one of the ones I never really got to read. I know he was interested in dance a lot.
